title: Exact Gaussian Moment Matching for Residual Networks: a Second-Order Method
claim: Moment-matched analytic propagation error shrinks faster than linearization as input uncertainty decreases, showing higher-order accuracy.
layout: 1 panel, log-scale x-axis decreasing left-to-right, two lines with markers
description: A single line plot on a log-scaled x-axis labeled 'Input covariance scale', running from 10^-1 on the left to 10^-8 on the right (decreasing). The y-axis has no tick labels, only light grid lines. Two series are shown. The orange dashed line with square markers is labeled 'linear' and falls steadily and almost linearly across the range. The blue solid line with circle markers is labeled 'analytic'. It stays below the orange line and falls more steeply, so the gap widens as the covariance scale shrinks. A legend in the top right names the two series. The grid is fine and gray, with minor log gridlines. The eye goes first to the widening gap between the blue and orange curves.
caption: Empirical small-covariance convergence for a fixed deep sine network. Methodology is described in Appendix [ref].
abstract: We study the problem of propagating the mean and covariance of a general multivariate Gaussian distribution through a deep (residual) neural network using layer-by-layer moment matching. We close a longstanding gap by deriving exact moment matching for the probit, GeLU, ReLU (as a limit of GeLU), Heaviside (as a limit of probit), and sine activation functions; for both feedforward and generalized residual layers. On large-variance random networks, median KL-divergence improvements over common baselines range from tens to thousands of times. On a variational Bayes neural network, we show that our method improves upon a state-of-the-art deterministic inference method by an order of magnitude in KL divergence from Monte Carlo ground truth. We also give a smooth-distance error bound showing that, under regularity assumptions, moment matching removes the leading low-variance errors and propagates higher-order local accuracy through the layers of a network.
